                       EXCEPTIONS TO THE PROPOSAL FOR DECISION
          Intervenors Dennis Grafa, Gary and Katherine Johnson, Tana Autrey, 9-Campbell Ranch,
 L.P., Sharon Holman as Trustee of the Charles Ray Pfluger Shelter Trust, Melissa O’Harrow and
 James Hamilton O’Harrow Family Trust, and Chase B. Akin (collectively “Link R1 Opposition
 Landowners” or “R1 Landowners”) respectfully and timely file these Exceptions to specific
 portions of the Proposal for Decision (“PFD”). R1 Landowners would respectfully show the
 following in support of same:


        I.    SUMMARY OF EXCEPTIONS IN PFD

          Link R1 Opposition Landowners recognize the difficult task set before the Administrative
 Law Judges (“ALJs”) in this voluminous and unprecedented Docket. 1 The compressed timeline
 and the sheer volume of evidence burdened the ALJs, the landowners, and counsel alike.
          The Public Utility Commission of Texas (“Commission”) should accept the PFD
 recommendation to deny the Application. Nevertheless, if the Commission does decline the
 recommendation to deny, it should also decline to adopt the PFD’s recommendation of Route 894




 1
  Proposal for Decision (August 20, 2026) at 6-7 (Over 1,000 intervenors); at 11-12 (823 submitted written testimonies,
 40 witnesses, 1,398 exhibits, 23 minutes to cross Applicant panel, 7 minutes to cross Commission Staff, and only 3
 minutes to cross Intervenor Witnesses)
                                                                                                                     3
 and should instead select Route 894 Western Mod. 1. 2 R1 Landowners except only to the PFD’s
routing-criteria analysis, which overlooked the superior performance of Route 894 Western Mod.
1 through the use of Links N12 and P1—a route advocated in R1 Landowners’ Initial and Reply
Briefs and supported by the record. 3 R1 Landowners take no exception to the PFD on Notice, Due
Process, or Need. 4
        R1 Landowners began disadvantaged: Link R1 appears in 85% of the 1,246 routes the
Applicants identified and in 78% of the 122 filed routes. 5 Route 894 Western Mod. 1 is a forward-
progressing and constructable RFI Route , yet the PFD wrongly set it aside on a single criterion—
that it “has less length parallel to existing compatible ROW than the Focus Routes.” 6 That criterion
rests on a single routing factor, the “apparent boundary lines” derived from tax-parcel data rather
than the actual property lines Commission Rule 25.101(b)(3)(B) requires. Measured correctly,
Route 894 Western Mod. 1 outperforms Route 894 on paralleling of compatible infrastructure,
community values, aesthetics, land use, and prudent avoidance, and performs substantially the
same on every remaining factor.


     V.       PRELIMINARY ORDER: ISSUES 1-4

        R1 Landowners propose no exceptions to this section and agree with the PFD.


    VI.       ISSUES RAISED BY THIRD PARTIES: DUE PROCESS

           R1 Landowners propose no exceptions to this section and agree with the PFD.


    VII.      NEED: ISSUES 5-7

        R1 Landowners propose no exceptions to this section and agree with the PFD.

      VIII.      ROUTING CRITERIA: ISSUES 8-10

           R1 Landowners except to Findings of Fact Nos. 160, 176, 178, 179, 180, 197, 223, and to
Conclusion of Law No. 16. The PFD recommends Route 894 after dismissing Route 894 Western
Mod. 1 on one flawed factor—parallel to existing compatible right-of-way—without balancing the
PURA factors. 7 The PFD should have further analyzed Route 894 Western Mod. 1 and not
categorically dismissed it. The record supports locating the Bell County to Big Hill 765-kV
transmission line (“Proposed Transmission Line”) along Route 894 Western Mod. 1.

    A. Overview – The PFD dismissed Route 894 Western Mod. 1 on a single, faulty
       paralleling metric rather than balancing all routing factors.
       The PFD states that no non-focus route, including Route 894 Western Mod. 1, presented a
clear advantage over the Focus Routes. The record shows otherwise: Route 894 Western Mod. 1
outperforms Route 894 and the other Central and Southern Corridor Routes on nearly every
criterion across the western quarter of the Study Area as addressed below. Route 894 Western
Mod. 1 is comprised of noticed links, and one of the nine routes of interest discussed at the Hearing
on the Merits (“Hearing”).

           The PFD correctly observes Route 894 Western Mod. 1 received less discussion than the
Focus Routes; however, it did receive sufficient attention to become a route of interest. The lack
of discussion is a function of geography and population, not merit. The two routes differ only
across the western quarter—roughly 25% of the Proposed Transmission Line—with far fewer
landowners and where the river crossings, parks, and population centers that dominated much of
the Hearing and briefing are absent. 8 A landowner supporting Route 894 who does not have land
in the West along Links N2, N11, N12, or P1 has no stake in the difference between the two routes,
so why would the landowner discuss it? Less attention is not a reason to dismiss a route’s
advantages, and the landowners of the western quarter are entitled to the same weight and analysis
as those anywhere else along the 200-plus-mile Proposed Transmission Line.
             Route 894 Western Mod. 1 carries the same advantages Route 894 has in the eastern portion
of the Study Area and adds material advantages in the west. Route 894 Western Mod. 1 modifies
Route 894 in the west, which can and should be done with other routes like Route 296 or 572.




7
    Id. at 107.
8

                                                                                                    5
      B. Concerns regarding routing methodology
         R1 Landowners propose no exceptions to this section and agree with the PFD.

     C. Community Values – The record supports selection of Route 894 Western
        Mod. 1.
         As the PFD explains, the Commission has described adverse effects upon community
values as “those aspects of a proposed project that would significantly alter the use, enjoyment, or
intrinsic value attached to an important area or resource by a community.” 9 In the western portion
of the Study Area, especially in the Central Corridor along Link N3 and R1, those values include
the protection of homes, the avoidance of bisection and fragmentation of working ranchland, and
the preservation of a ranching heritage. 10 Community values also vary within the western quarter
itself: Concho County and portions of Tom Green County have embraced industrial infrastructure
such as wind farms, while landowners along Links N3 and R1 have consistently rejected that
change in land use. 11
         Finding of Fact No. 176 incorrectly concludes that Route 894 adequately addresses the
community values expressed in this record, particularly in the western quarter of the Study Area 12.
Although there are shared community values along the entire Project, Community values can and
do vary across the more than 200 miles and are expressed at both a county-wide and “neighborhood
scale”—a distinction the PFD does not address. 13 Additionally, although some of the community
values in the east and west are the same, naturally the east and west are different and the use and
values in these areas can and do change. The PFD correctly states concerns were expressed about
the negative impacts the Proposed Transmission Line would have on residences, ranching
operations, and the overall aesthetics. 14 Harm to residences, ranching operations, and aesthetics
are exactly the community values along Links R1 and N3, which would be impacted by the use of
Route 894. Route 894 would permanently alter the use, enjoyment, and intrinsic value of that
ranchland; Applicants’ EA data identify five homes along its Links N3, P2, and R1. 15 Links N12

identifies further homes just beyond the 500-foot band that the line would nonetheless affect. 17
        The PFD’s community-values analysis also omits existing and committed land use. Links
N12 and P1 used in Route 894 Western Mod. 1 are already affected by industrial infrastructure
(wind farms/turbines), and at least one intervenor on 894 Western Mod. 1 has leased the very land
Link P1 would cross for future wind or solar development. 18

             2. Impact to Landowners. Route 894 Western Mod. 1 reduces the impact to
                 landowners.

        Route 894 Western Mod. 1 crosses three more miles of rangeland pasture than Route 894
(165.8 versus 162.8 miles). 19 The PFD did not weigh against that difference the facts that Route
894 Western Mod. 1 traverses an existing wind farm, parallels substantially more existing
transmission line, and crosses land along Link P1 that its own owner has committed to a wind
and/or solar lease. Route 894’s Links N3 and R1, by contrast, place the line in the “backyards” of
numerous families, at least ten, and across the pastures on which their livelihoods depend.
        The PFD does not address the effect of Link R1 on Chase Akin’s West Texas Photo Safari,
a zoo, and a retreat with brand new facilities and improvements. Route 894 would bisect the Akin
ranch, which is home to numerous species of animals, and would devastate both the property and
the current and future use which relies on the land use and unadulterated aesthetics. 20
        The PFD does not address landowner preference where a single landowner is crossed by
more than one link. Angell Land and Livestock is bisected by both Link N3 and Link N12 and
prefers Link N12, which crosses his ranch in a less damaging location and affects no homes or
ranch residents. 21 The Charles Ray Pfluger Shelter Trust is likewise crossed by both Link R1 and
Link P1 and prefers Link P1, which follows an actual boundary line, versus bisecting the improved
ranch with Link R1.

          Links N3 and R1 fragment land that is presently unfragmented. Nearly every landowner
along Link N3 intervened, as did seven along Link R1, and each is partially or wholly bisected. 22
         In each instance, the PFD credited the Applicants’ EA data on “apparent boundary lines”
over the sworn testimony of the landowners who occupy the land and know where its boundaries
actually run.

             3. Future Development.

         Future development is not a reason to avoid Route 894 Western Mod. 1. No party reported
that “future development that could be affected [by] a proposed route has initiated in some readily
observable or measurable way on that route.” 23 Planned use nevertheless bears on landowners’
intent to impact land use, aesthetics, and community values. Landowners along Links N3 and R1
testified that they have refused every offer from renewable energy developers; Link N12, by
contrast, can be routed safely through an existing wind farm. 24 A large landowner opposing Route
894 Western Mod. 1 has recently leased the same Link P1 land for wind and/or solar development
that it now seeks to keep the Proposed Transmission Line off of. 25 The Commission should weigh
that evidence of intended future use in its community values and land-use analysis.

     D. Recreational and Park Areas
         R1 Landowners propose no exceptions to this section, as Route 894 Western Mod. 1
performs identically to Route 894.

     E. Aesthetic and Historic Values
         R1 Landowners except to Finding of Fact No. 197, which concludes that Route 894
reasonably minimizes aesthetic impacts while balancing the Commission’s routing criteria. 26
Route 894 introduces new industrial structures into an undisturbed viewshed. Route 894 Western
Mod. 1 uses Link N12, which runs through an existing wind farm, and therefore does not
substantially alter the character of the existing view for a portion of this route. The PFD gave that
evidence no weight, despite testimony from that routing through the existing wind farm would
reduce aesthetic impacts.

          In Concho County, wind towers stand on both sides for a portion of Link N12.
Transmission structures placed on N12 are absorbed into an already industrialized landscape,
rather than creating a new and permanent visual intrusion along the entire length of Link N3. 27
         The Applicants have built such transmission lines, plan to build other transmission lines,
and can build this Proposed Transmission Line through the wind farm along Link N12. 28 Just
recently, in Docket No. 59315, the Commission found that a link routed through wind turbines
“integrated the transmission towers into the same visual plane as the nearest other visual
disturbance of similar size.” 29 Although not to the same degree, this can occur here.
         The Commission can also materially reduce the aesthetic harm of the Proposed
Transmission Line in the rural western quarter by paralleling existing transmission lines 30,
avoiding the homes located on these properties, and routing through existing wind farms and land
that landowners along Link P1 have already committed to similar structures under leases spanning
decades. Route 894 Western Mod. 1 does each of these things in the western quarter; Route 894
does not.

     F. Environmental Integrity – The PFD did not consider the resident golden
        eagles along Link R1
         The PFD’s environmental-integrity analysis relies on the Applicants’ EA data regarding
bald eagles and does not address the on-the-ground testimony of Helen Dockal of 9-Campbell
Ranch, who identified an established pair of nesting golden eagles whose habitat lies just south of
Link R1. 31 Finding of Fact No. 220 extends protection to raptors, like golden eagles. R1
Landowners except to Finding of Fact No. 223. Route 894 Western Mod. 1 avoids the habitat and
nesting area for these eagles on Link R1 entirely and eliminates any risk of disturbance during and
after construction.
         The PFD also does not address the five federally endangered, threatened, or vulnerable
species held on the Akin property—clouded leopard, white rhinoceros, Arabian oryx, white-
handed gibbon, and cheetah. 32 That the property is not their native range does not make it any less

importance and on the impact to landowners.

     G. Costs
         R1 Landowners take no exception to the PFD’s determination that cost is not a
distinguishing factor. The PFD did, however, pass over evidence of cost savings available from
link combinations other than N3-P2-R1. 33 Link using N3-R1 are more expensive on a cost-per-
mile basis.
         Using the same analysis as in the PFD, Route 894 Western Mod. 1’s cost estimate for the
Proposed Transmission Line is $1,695,280,468, which is $14.36 million more (0.85%) than Route
894 34. This is 3.6% above the cheapest route. That difference buys avoidance of at least five
habitable structures, materially better performance on community values, and no new
fragmentation across the western quarter.

     H. Engineering Constraints
         Route 894 Western Mod. 1 also performs better on engineering constraints, particularly
aviation. Both routes affect the same three FAA airports with runways longer than 3,200 feet
within 20,000 feet of the centerline, but Route 894 Western Mod. 1 affects no private airstrips
within 10,000 feet of its centerline, while Route 894 affects two. 35
         The PFD acknowledges but then dismisses the helipad roughly 3,000 feet north of Link N3
on the Rancho Bonito property, which the Menard County Constable uses regularly for emergency
and law-enforcement operations. Route 894 Western Mod. 1 avoids Link N3 and has no helipad
in its vicinity. The PFD likewise does not address the ground-troop and helicopter training Rancho
Bonito has provided the military for years. 36

     I. Route Length and Use of Compatible Right-of-Ways/Property Lines
         R1 Landowners except to Findings of Fact Nos. 178, 179, and 180. Commission Rule
25.101(b)(3)(B)(i)-(iii) requires consideration of paralleling “property lines,” not apparent
property lines. The PFD itself acknowledges that tax-parcel boundary data does not always reflect
the full extent of a landowner’s contiguous property and is therefore an imperfect metric. 37 That

   defect is likely not uniform. In the more densely subdivided eastern portion of the Study Area, tax-
  parcel data likely approximates real boundaries. In the western quarter, a single contiguous ranch
  frequently carries several tax-parcel identifications, so a line that appears on paper to follow a
  boundary in fact bisects the property. The metric therefore systematically disadvantages the large
  and rural tracts. The Applicants did the best they could with the available data, but it is not a
  standard the Commission should apply in a case of this magnitude—the same limitations of county
  appraisal district data the parties addressed in the notice context apply here. Actual proper lines
  matter, not apparent.

  look to paralleling of existing compatible infrastructure—roads, highways, and transmission
  lines—a point the PFD acknowledged. 38 That infrastructure is consistently mapped across the
  Study Area in known data sets, but the PFD applied the measure only to Routes 392 and 894.

  Route 894, which parallels only 10.1 miles 39. Route 894 Western Mod. 1 parallels 12.2 miles of
  compatible infrastructure, 5.37% of its total length. 40

          Paralleling of existing transmission line rights-of-way also mitigates aesthetic impact.
Route 894 Western Mod. 1 parallels 9.8 miles of existing transmission line, 4.1 miles more than
Route 894 because of using the N2-N11-N12 link sequence. 41
         Because the “apparent” boundary lines underlying the Applicants’ EA totals are frequently
not boundary lines at all, neither the PFD nor the Commission should treat total length paralleling
as dispositive.

     J. Prudent Avoidance
         Population centers differ across the Study Area. In the east they are towns and
communities; in the western quarter they are individual homes and ranch headquarters.

         Route 894 Western Mod. 1 better satisfies prudent avoidance because it limits exposure to
electric and magnetic fields at a reasonable investment of money and effort. It affects 80 habitable
structures, tying for the lowest count of any route, and using Links N12 and P1 in 894 Western
Mod. 1 do not trade one set of habitable structures for another—they contain none. 42 Plus, there
are the additional benefits of the other routing factors such as land use, community values,
aesthetics, and paralleling of compatible infrastructure as discussed herein. 894 Western Mod. 1
better complies with Prudent Avoidance than Route 894 does. Avoiding these habitable structures,
these gathering places, and lacing the Proposed Transmission Line along N12 and P1 is a
reasonable alternative to avoid and limit the exposure to electric and magnetic fields. Because the
PFD found cost not to be a distinguishing factor, that avoidance is by definition a reasonable
investment of money and effort.

     K. Moderation of Impact to Landowners
         R1 Landowners propose no exceptions to this section.

     L. Routing Recommendation
         Because cost and length are not distinguishing factors, neither can defeat Route 894
Western Mod. 1. The choice therefore turns on the remaining criteria, and on those criteria where
Route 894 Western Mod. 1 outperforms Route 894 and other routes in the western quarter.
         Route 894 avoids Florence Elementary School; it ties for the lowest habitable-structure
count of any route and places no structure at all along Links N12 and P1, which is a core of prudent
avoidance and the community value landowners voiced most often;

 Link R1 Reply Brief at 22-23, 26
41

 There is also an additional habitable structure on Link N3 on MK3 land that was not discussed; use of 894 Western
42

Mod. 1 also avoids this habitable structure
                                                                                                               12
            Route 894 Western Mod. 1’s centerline runs no closer than 1,000 feet to any park or
recreational area and outside the one-half-mile foreground visual zone of each.
          Route 894 Western Mod. 1 parallels more existing compatible infrastructure—the measure
the Commission should credit, given the acknowledged unreliability of apparent boundary lines—
all while partially routing through an existing wind farm that absorbs its visual impact.


       IX.      CONCLUSION

           The advantages of Route 894 Western Mod. 1 lie in using Links N12 and P1; and these
links/advantages are available to any route. Each Focus Route—296, 487, and 894—and each
other route of interest discussed at the Hearing, including 572 and Cherokee Creek G, can be
modified to use Links N12 and/or P1 43. The Commission need not take any route “as is,” and it
should not do so at the cost of disregarding the record concerning the western quarter of the
Proposed Transmission Line.
           The Commission should accept the PFD’s recommendation to deny the Proposed
Transmission Line Project; however, if a route must be selected, then for the foregoing reasons,
Link R1 Opposition Landowners respectfully request that the Commission reject the PFD’s
recommendation of Route 894 and instead select Route 894 Western Mod. 1, or a modification of
any other route—such as Route 296 or Route 572—that uses Links N12 and/or P1.

   VIII.        ROUTING CRITERIA: ISSUES 8-10

          Rl Landowners except to Findings of Fact Nos. 160, 176, 178, 179, 180, 197, 223, and to
Conclusion of Law No. 16. The PFD recommends Route 894 after dismissing Route 894 Western
Mod. 1 on one flawed factor-parallel to existing compatible right-of-way-without balancing the
PURA factors.7 The PFD should have further analyzed Route 894 Western Mod. 1 and not
categorically dismissed it. The record supports locating the Bell County to Big Hill 765-kV
transmission line ("Proposed Transmission Line") along Route 894 Western Mod. 1.

  A. Overview - The PFD dismissed Route 894 Western Mod. 1 on a single, faulty
       paralleling metric rather than balancing all routing factors.
    The PFD states that no non-focus route, including Route 894 Western Mod. 1, presented a
clear advantage over the Focus Routes. The record shows otherwise: Route 894 Western Mod. 1
outperforms Route 894 and the other Central and Southern Corridor Routes on nearly every
criterion across the western quarter of the Study Area as addressed below. Route 894 Western
Mod. 1 is comprised of noticed links, and one ofthe nine routes ofinterest discussed at the Hearing
on the Merits ("Hearing").

          The PFD correctly observes Route 894 Western Mod. 1 received less discussion than the
Focus Routes; however, it did receive sufficient attention to become a route of interest. The lack
of discussion is a function of geography and population, not merit. The two routes differ only
across the western quarter-roughly 25% of the Proposed Transmission Line-with far fewer
landowners and where the river crossings, parks, and population centers that dominated much of
the Hearing and briefing are absent. 8 A landowner supporting Route 894 who does not have land
in the West along Links N2, Nll, N12, or P1 has no stake in the difference between the two routes,
so why would the landowner discuss it? Less attention is not a reason to dismiss a route's
advantages, and the landowners of the western quarter are entitled to the same weight and analysis
as those anywhere else along the 200-plus-mile Proposed Transmission Line.
          Route 894 Western Mod. 1 carries the same advantages Route 894 has in the eastern portion
of the Study Area and adds material advantages in the west. Route 894 Western Mod. 1 modifies
Route 894 in the west, which can and should be done with other routes like Route 296 or 572.

  J. Prudent Avoidance
        Population centers differ across the Study Area. In the east they are towns and
communities; in the western quarter they are individual homes and ranch headquarters.

        Route 894 Western Mod. 1 better satisfies prudent avoidance because it limits exposure to
electric and magnetic fields at a reasonable investment of money and effort. It affects 80 habitable
structures, tying for the lowest count of any route, and using Links N12 and Pl in 894 Western
Mod. 1 do not trade one set of habitable structures for another-they contain none.42 Plus, there
are the additional benefits of the other routing factors such as land use, community values,
aesthetics, and paralleling of compatible infrastructure as discussed herein. 894 Western Mod. 1
better complies with Prudent Avoidance than Route 894 does. Avoiding these habitable structures,
these gathering places, and lacing the Proposed Transmission Line along N12 and Pl is a
reasonable alternative to avoid and limit the exposure to electric and magnetic fields. Because the
PFD found cost not to be a distinguishing factor, that avoidance is by definition a reasonable
investment of money and effort.

    IX.      CONCLUSION

          The advantages of Route 894 Western Mod. 1 lie in using Links N12 and Pl; and these
links/advantages are available to any route. Each Focus Route-296,487, and 894-and each
other route of interest discussed at the Hearing, including 572 and Cherokee Creek G, can be
modified to use Links N12 and/or P143. The Commission need not take any route "as is, " and it
should not do so at the cost of disregarding the record concerning the western quarter of the
Proposed Transmission Line.
          The Commission should accept the PFD's recommendation to deny the Proposed
Transmission Line Project; however, if a route must be selected, then for the foregoing reasons,
Link Rl Opposition Landowners respectfully request that the Commission reject the PFD's
recommendation of Route 894 and instead select Route 894 Western Mod. 1, or a modification of
any other route-such as Route 296 or Route 572-that uses Links N12 and/or Pl.
